title: Yoga, the boat to Brahman
hookLine: seekers ask where everything comes from, and the Shvetashvatara answers by teaching them to sit: the body as a boat to Brahman
carry: yoga is the boat to brahman
last: GOD IS IN YOU LIKE FIRE IN WOOD.

cards: A circle of seekers once sat together with the biggest questions there are. What is the cause of everything? Where do we come from?
What holds our lives up? The Shvetashvatara Upanishad opens with them. And here's the turn: they didn't settle it by arguing.
Following the yoga of meditation, the text says, they saw God's own power hidden in the world. So when this book teaches you how to sit, it isn't a fitness tip. It's the seekers' boat.

teach.b: Verse 2.8, in paraphrase: holding the body steady, chest, neck and head upright, and drawing the senses and the mind into the heart, the wise one crosses the frightening rivers on the boat of Brahman.

teach.h: BREATH SOFT, GROUND LEVEL AND CLEAN.
teach.b: Verse 2.9 takes the breath: quiet it, and breathe out through the nose once it has grown soft. Then hold the mind the way a driver holds a chariot yoked to wild horses, alert, never careless.

Verse 2.10 chooses the place: level and clean, free of pebbles, fire and sand, pleasing to the mind, near the sound of water, sheltered from the wind. Charmingly human: no gravel under you, no smoke in your eyes.
Here's the teaching. The word yoga comes from a root meaning to yoke, to join, the same yoking as those horses. In Hinduism the straight spine and the soft breath were never the goal.
They settle the body so the senses can turn inward, toward the self and toward God.

The posture is the boat; Brahman is the far shore. The book closes by naming its teacher, the sage Shvetashvatara, who, it says, knew Brahman through his discipline and the grace of God, and passed it on.
So a yoga class at the gym can be just exercise, and that's fine. But in this tradition, sitting still was always meant to carry you across.

how: Hindus who meditate may sit cross-legged or on a chair with the chest, neck and head in one line, choose a clean, quiet corner, and soften the breath before turning attention inward, much as Shvetashvatara 2.8–2.10 describes.

o: a breathing count used to calm the mind
a seat, the steady posture for meditation
a hard stretch held to build up strength

games.q: verse by verse: tap the pairs.
p: chest, neck and head held upright
the breath softened; the mind like wild horses
a clean, level, quiet, sheltered place
carries the meditator across the rivers

s: the Shvetashvatara's instructions are only about the mind, not the body
2.8 starts with the body: chest, neck and head held upright, then the senses drawn in.
the text likes a spot near the pleasant sound of water
2.10, as most translators read it, wants a place pleasing to the mind, with the sound of water, sheltered from the wind.
the verses that follow promise lightness and health as first signs
2.13 lists lightness, health, a clear complexion and a pleasant voice.

games.q: a friend's yoga teacher says yoga is 'just stretching, nothing spiritual'. what would the Shvetashvatara add?
o: the posture is a boat: body steady, senses gathered, mind turned toward Brahman.
that yoga is only for priests, so nobody else should do it.
that the deeper the stretch, the closer you get to God.
games.why: 2.8: with the body upright and the senses drawn into the heart, the wise cross the frightening rivers on the boat of Brahman. the seat serves the crossing.

practice: Stack the three, chest lifted, neck long, head balanced on top, and let the breath grow soft and leave through the nose. Then gather the senses in, as if eyes, ears and skin were drawing back toward the heart.
If a horse bolts, a thought or a sound, take the reins gently. If you pray, let the stillness carry you toward the one you pray to; if you don't, let the breath be the boat.

wordCard.voice: Asana, seat, posture. In the Shvetashvatara, the steady seat that becomes a boat: upright from chest to head, senses drawn into the heart.

orig.note: Sanskrit āsana: seat, posture. the word the Yoga Sutras will later define as 'steady and comfortable'.

carryVoice: Your line: yoga is the boat to Brahman. The body steady, the mind turned in. That's day four hundred twenty-five.
